page.h1: HTS Chapter 02: Meat and Edible Meat Offal — U.S. Exports & Foreign Tariffs

seo.title: Chapter 02 U.S. Meat Exports: Who Buys & Foreign Tariffs
seo.shortDescription: How much beef, pork and poultry the U.S. exports, who buys it, and what each top buyer charges, from 2020–2025 UN Comtrade data.

intro:
The U.S. exported **$21.31 billion** of Chapter 02 goods in 2025, down **6.0%** from 2024. **Pork (heading 0203) is 30%** of that, **poultry (0207) 22%** and **beef (0201 and 0202 together) 38%**. Mexico, South Korea and Japan buy **51%** of the chapter. The drop is mostly China, whose purchases fell **52.5%** to $1.34 billion.

Tariffs matter in two places. China charges its normal rate on meat plus an extra 10% on every U.S. good. Japan still charges about 21% on U.S. beef even under the trade agreement, falling to 9% by 2033. Almost everywhere else, U.S. meat is free or phasing to free under a U.S. trade agreement (Mexico, Canada, South Korea, Colombia, the Dominican Republic) or under a free-port regime (Hong Kong). Taiwan, a mid-sized buyer, agreed in February 2026 to cut its tariffs on U.S. beef and pork, but the cuts are not yet confirmed in force. What usually decides access is health approval, such as plant eligibility and certificates, not a tariff.

keyTakeaways: Pork, poultry and beef are about 90% of this chapter: pork (0203) 30%, poultry (0207) 22% and beef (0201 and 0202) 38%.

Most large buyers charge little or nothing: Mexico, Canada, South Korea and Hong Kong are essentially duty-free, and Colombia and the Dominican Republic are free within quotas. Japan is the exception on beef, at about 21%.

China is the one top buyer that raised tariffs. It lifted its 10–15% tariffs on U.S. pork, beef and chicken on November 10, 2025, but its extra 10% on all U.S. goods stays, and purchases fell 52.5% in 2025.
The U.S. side is routine: a Schedule B number, an USDA FSIS export certificate from an eligible plant, buyer screening and an AES filing. No export licence applies in the ordinary case.
